quote: Diese Bemerkung hat viel- leicht zur Folge die Gültigkeit folgenden einfachen Satzes: Wenn $f(x)$ stetig und periodisch ist und die mit den Fourierschen Coefficienten $\int_{-\pi}^{+\pi} f(x) \cos nx\, dx$ gebildete Fouriersche Reihe convergirt, so stellt sie die Funktion $f(x)$ dar.
english: This remark perhaps implies the validity of the following simple theorem: if f(x) is continuous and periodic and the Fourier series formed with the Fourier coefficients ∫_{-π}^{+π} f(x) cos nx dx converges, then it represents the function f(x).
topic: A garden-division minimum problem, quotations from Kronecker's lectures on definite integrals (Darwinian analogy, functions of one variable as limit cases, Fourier double integral, passage to Poisson's integral via Abel's theorem, a convergence theorem for Fourier series), and the Codazzi formulas applied to Hilbert's theorem on surfaces of constant negative curvature.

triage.modern_statement: Let f be a continuous 2π-periodic function with Fourier coefficients a_n = (1/π)∫_{-π}^{π} f(x) cos nx dx and b_n = (1/π)∫_{-π}^{π} f(x) sin nx dx. The claim is that if the Fourier series of f converges at a point x (or everywhere), then its sum at x equals f(x). In other words, wherever the Fourier series of a continuous function converges, it converges to that function. The claim does not say the series always converges, and in general it does not.
triage.answered_by: The claim is true, and it is now a standard textbook fact. The usual proof follows from Fejér's theorem (L. Fejér, 1900): the Cesàro (C,1) means of the Fourier series of a continuous periodic f converge uniformly to f. A convergent series is Cesàro-summable to the same limit, so wherever the Fourier series converges, its sum must be f(x). The route Hilbert's note points to also works: by Abel's theorem, a convergent series equals its Abel sum, and the Poisson integral (the Abel means) tends to f(x) at points where f is continuous. That gives the same conclusion. The searches did not turn up a source giving the precise date and author of the Abel–Poisson version, so I give no attribution for it. The statement is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Fejér proved in 1900 that the Fourier series of a continuous periodic function is Cesàro-summable to the function.
Fejér's theorem: for continuous 2π-periodic f, the Cesàro means σ_n(f) converge uniformly to f. If s_n converges to s, then σ_n also converges to s.
A textbook-style write-up states the consequence directly: if the partial sums S_N(x) converge, the means σ_N(x) converge to the same limit, and Fejér's theorem makes that limit the function itself.
The hypothesis that the series converges is genuinely needed: du Bois-Reymond (1873) built a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point.
General background on the many sufficient conditions for Fourier series to converge (Dirichlet–Jordan, Hölder conditions, and others).

triage.why: Hilbert's 'simple theorem' is correct, and it became a routine corollary once summability methods were in use. Fejér's 1900 Cesàro theorem gives it directly, and the Abel/Poisson route that Kronecker's lecture suggests (Abel's theorem plus Poisson's integral) works as well. It is a standard textbook fact, not an open problem. Research on pointwise convergence of Fourier series continues, but on other questions such as divergence and almost-everywhere convergence, not on this statement.
